lesson_title: Equivalent Descriptions of the Same Relationship
hook_text: A map, a timetable, a text. Same bus.
clip_script:
Think about a bus trip from Durban to Pietermaritzburg. You could describe it with a map — a line between two dots with the road drawn in. You could describe it with a timetable — departs seven, arrives eight fifteen, stops at Pinetown and Hillcrest. You could describe it with a text message — leaving now, be there by quarter past eight. Three descriptions, one journey. The map is good for seeing where you go; the timetable for knowing when; the message for telling someone quickly. Nobody thinks these are three different journeys.

A relationship in mathematics is the same. The hall-hire cost is one thing. Five hundred plus forty a head is the text message — quick, in words. The flow diagram is the map — it shows the route the number takes, multiply then add. The table is the timetable — specific stops: ten guests, nine hundred; twenty, one thousand three hundred. The formula is the complete route description that lets you work out any stop.
visual_style: A road map, a printed timetable and a phone screen side by side, all describing one bus; then a flow diagram, a table and a formula side by side describing one cost rule
call_to_action: Open the full session to translate any relationship between words, diagrams, tables, formulas and equations.
